This could be due to the base case conduction and convection already provided a good drying rate and US application was not effective in providing additional water removal. It is clear from the ultrasonic experiments that US applications in conjunction with convection are more effective at lower basis weights and throughout the drying period. US applications in the pockets (along with convection) after conduction on the cylinders are more favorable resulting reasonable improvements in drying rate and energy intensity for all basis weights studied. This suggests adding US in the pockets with pocket ventilation systems might be the desired approach. It should be noted that there are practical limitations related to applying US, especially contact US, in the pockets and they warrant further exploration. The optimal integration of RF and US in conjunction with alternating conduction and convection drying (i.e. multi-cylinder drying) was then evaluated. With optimal integration of RFUS technology we were able to alter the drying rate profile and improve the overall drying performance. Results clearly showed that with optimum integration of RFUS at various locations on the paper machine, the desired target improvements in drying rate and drying time achieving the project goals. Basic description of the paper drying transport model considering the mass, energy and momentum transport with associated governing equations, initial and boundary conditions was completed. The mathematical model is solved using multi-physics, computational simulation approaches. The overall average drying rate from the simulations for different grades of paper were compared with commercial data from the industry sponsors and literature and, in general, there was a good agreement between the simulation results and the commercial data. In addition, the instantaneous heating up and colling of the sheet and the corresponding variations in drying rate as well as the overall average drying rate matched well with the experimental data. Appropriate model parameters including the liquid permeability, gas permeability, diffusivity, 58 DE-EE0009395 heat and mass transfer coefficients were determined based on the comparison with experimental data. The experimental data from the periodic application of RF and US in conjunction with conduction and convection drying was then simulated with the model. Based on these simulations, necessary RF and US conditions and integration with multi-cylinder drying is determined for achieving target improvements in overall drying rates. These results confirm with experimental data demonstrating the benefits of RFUS with uniform volumetric heating and water removal resulting in higher drying rates, shorter falling rate period and increased drying rates during the entire drying periods including the falling rate period. Based on experimental data and modeling and simulation results, we have shown that with optimal integration of the RFUS, we can achieve necessary improvements in drying rates compared to the base case conduction and convection, reaching the minimum and stretch target improvements in overall drying rates.
